idiom_name: asSequence()/sequence { } chain with map/filter/take, forced by a terminal operator
implementation_notes: kotlin.sequences is the stdlib realisation: a Sequence produces elements while it is iterated, intermediate operators (map/filter/flatMap/drop/take, plus stateful ones such as distinct/groupBy/sortedBy) return another lazy Sequence and terminal operators (toList/sum/fold/first/max) both drive the chain and define the sink. Sources are anything asSequence()-able, generateSequence, or a sequence { yield(...) } builder, and what replaces the classic structure is precisely the intermediate/terminal split: the terminal supplies the accumulator semantics, so no reducing-function transformer is needed and laziness is preserved through the chain. The classic transducer shape is justified only when one transformation must also drive a non-Sequence sink (a Channel, a callback API) or has to be published as a value of a single type.
pitfalls: Sequences are lazy and the documentation warns the overhead can outweigh the gain for small collections or simple operations - an Iterable chain is often faster there.
Nothing runs without a terminal operator, and a sequence captured from a scoped resource (a reader inside useLines/use) escapes after the resource is closed.
Most sequences can be iterated repeatedly, but some generateSequence overloads throw on the second iteration - state the traversal contract explicitly.

variants.name: Flow pipeline (kotlinx.coroutines)
variants.implementation_notes: Flow is the asynchronous version of the same idea: a cold stream of values whose intermediate operators (map/filter/take/zip/...) return a new downstream Flow and whose terminal operators (collect/fold/reduce/first/toList/launchIn) trigger execution. Every flow step is a suspend function, so a stage can await I/O, and a cold flow re-executes for every collector - which is what makes the transformation value safe to publish, unlike a one-shot stateful transducer. Concurrency is explicit: buffer/conflate overlap upstream and downstream, flowOn moves upstream work to another dispatcher while preserving the downstream context, and the collector's suspension provides backpressure. What replaces the classic structure: the transformation is a Flow -> Flow function and the sink is the collector; there is no reducing-function protocol to hand-roll and no intermediate collections to avoid, but the pipeline is now tied to kotlinx.coroutines.
variants.code_sketch:
val pages: Flow<Page> = flow { for (u in urls) emit(fetch(u)) }      // cold, suspending
val titles = pages
    .filter { it.isValid }
    .map { it.title }              // intermediate: returns a new downstream Flow
    .buffer(4)                     // run upstream concurrently with collection
titles.onEach(::print).launchIn(scope)     // terminal operator starts collection
pitfalls: A cold flow restarts for every collector - three collectors mean three fetches; share with stateIn/shareIn (or a channel) when the source must run once.
Flow operators run in the collector's context unless flowOn is used; blocking calls or runBlocking inside a flow break structured concurrency and can starve the dispatcher.
Cancellation must propagate: catching CancellationException inside an operator breaks cancellation, and emitting from an arbitrary coroutine requires channelFlow/send rather than flow.
